title: Monitoring your portfolio: how often should you check
subtitle: Monitoring frequency
openingQuestion: Linh invests long-term in a diversified portfolio of index funds and stocks for a retirement goal 20 years away, but has a habit of opening the app to check her portfolio's value 5-10 times a day, losing sleep with worry every time she sees red. What effect does this habit have on her long-term investment results?
openingOptions: You should only check your portfolio exactly once, right when you first start investing, and never look at it again after that
Checking too often easily leads to emotional decisions, doing more harm than good
Checking the portfolio more frequently helps you react faster to the market, so it's always beneficial for long-term investment performance
How often you check the portfolio has absolutely no effect on decision-making behavior or the investor's final results
explanation: Many behavioral finance studies show that the more often an investor checks their portfolio, the more susceptible they become to short-term swings (called 'myopic loss aversion'), leading to emotional decisions like selling out during a temporary drop or chasing prices during a hot rally - both of which run counter to a disciplined long-term strategy. For a long-term goal (retirement, a child's education fund), a sensible checking frequency is usually monthly or quarterly - enough to track progress and rebalance when needed, without being so frequent that it triggers overreacting to short-term noise.

realWorldExample.description: When the VN-Index dropped sharply in 2022 (from a peak of around 1,500 points to below 900), many individual investors who watched the price board constantly sold out at low prices out of panic, while those who checked less often or held to a disciplined long-term approach (on a schedule, not reacting to short-term swings) usually held their portfolio through the difficult period and benefited when the market recovered afterward.

quiz.question: Why can checking an investment portfolio too often (many times a day) HARM long-term investment results?
options: Because seeing a lot of swings makes emotional reactions easy
Because the system only updates the exact price once a day
Because looking often slows down the account's order execution speed
Because every time you check the portfolio, a query fee is charged
quiz.explanation: The phenomenon of 'myopic loss aversion' makes someone who tracks fluctuations frequently feel more risk and worry than the reality warrants, easily leading to a mistaken, emotion-driven decision instead of sticking to the long-term plan.

quiz.question: What checking frequency is usually recommended for a long-term investment goal (10-20 years)?
options: Multiple times a day so nothing is missed
Monthly or quarterly is enough
Once a day at market close
Just once, after 10 years
quiz.explanation: Checking monthly/quarterly lets an investor track progress and rebalance when the weighting drifts too far from target, without getting swept up in daily price noise.

quiz.question: Why is checking the portfolio too often harmful?
options: Because the system only updates the portfolio's exact value once a month
Because the brokerage charges a fee every time you log in to view the portfolio
Because seeing a lot of short-term swings raises the chance of selling out of fear
Because checking often is assumed to lower the recorded investment performance shown in the account
quiz.explanation: The more often you look, the more red sessions you see - even though the long-term trend hasn't changed. This is 'myopic loss aversion': the frequency of looking determines the feeling of risk more than the portfolio itself does.

quiz.question: What's a sensible frequency for a long-term investor to review their portfolio?
options: Every time major news about the stock market appears in the press
Once a day, at the close of each session, to closely track market moves
Exactly once, on the last day before retiring
Every few months, enough to rebalance without getting swept up in the news
quiz.explanation: Sparse enough to avoid reacting to noise, frequent enough not to miss a needed rebalance or a genuine change in your own circumstances. Six months to a year is what most long-term plans actually need.

quiz.question: When reviewing your portfolio, what's the most worthwhile question to ask?
options: Is the weighting still on target, and is that target still right for my life
Which ticker is up the most, and should I buy more of it right now
Will the market go up or down next week, so I can time a trade
How many percentage points is my portfolio lagging my friends and colleagues by
quiz.explanation: Those two questions are about you, not about the market - and they're the only two things you actually control. The other questions all lead to acting on something nobody can predict.

quiz.question: How does checking your portfolio differ from reacting to news?
options: Checking can only be done by professionals, reacting is for individuals
Checking follows a pre-set schedule; reacting is action driven by emotion
The two are the same thing, just called differently depending on the market situation
Checking lowers returns while reacting quickly to news raises them
quiz.explanation: A pre-set schedule separates the decision from the emotion: you decide before you know what the market will do. Reacting to news is the opposite - and it's how most individual investors end up buying high and selling low.

keyTakeaways: Checking the portfolio too often doesn't improve performance - it makes emotional decisions more likely, hurting a long-term strategy
A sensible frequency for a long-term goal (retirement, a child's education) is monthly or quarterly
Turning off daily price-movement notifications on an investing app is a simple way to reduce the temptation to check constantly
A periodic check should come with a clear purpose: tracking progress toward the goal and rebalancing when needed, not just to 'see if it's up or down'

practicePrompt.question: Linh is investing for a retirement goal 20 years away but has a habit of checking her portfolio 8 times a day and often losing sleep with worry when she sees red. What advice best helps her improve this habit while still tracking progress toward her goal?
options: Turn off daily price-movement notifications on the app, and only review the portfolio once a month or once a quarter
Keep checking 8 times a day as she currently does, since that's the only way to react in time to every market move
Stop tracking the portfolio entirely for the next 20 years, with no review needed until the exact day she retires
Switch to checking the portfolio hourly instead of daily, to react even faster to small fluctuations
practicePrompt.explanation: Turning off notifications and lowering the frequency to monthly/quarterly is still enough to track progress and rebalance when needed, while reducing the temptation to react emotionally to short-term swings.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Try it now
application.message: Open your investing app, turn off all daily price-movement notifications, and set yourself a reminder to only check the portfolio again at the start of next month.
application.secondary: You'll be surprised how much less anxious you feel once you stop watching the price every day.

sections.text: Technology lets us see a portfolio's value anytime, anywhere - but being able to do that doesn't mean you should do it often. For long-term investing, checking too frequently can backfire.

Successful long-term investing usually doesn't come from reacting quickly to every swing, but from sticking to a strategy through multiple market cycles. The paradox is: someone who checks their portfolio less often sometimes ends up with better results, simply because they have fewer opportunities to make an emotion-driven mistake.
Myopic loss aversion - why checking often is harmful

In behavioral finance, 'myopic loss aversion' describes people's tendency to feel the pain of a loss far more strongly than the pleasure of an equivalent gain. When checking a portfolio daily or several times a day, an investor keeps witnessing short-term drops (even if it's just normal market fluctuation), building up anxiety, and becoming more likely to sell out even though the portfolio is still on track over the long run.

items: Checking daily: easy to see short-term swings, raises anxiety, easy to react emotionally
Checking monthly: enough to track the trend, reduces the impact of short-term noise
Checking quarterly/twice a year: suits a portfolio that's already stable, only needing periodic rebalancing
Checking annually: suits a long-term retirement fund, mainly to review the overall goal

sections.label: An exception worth noting
sections.text: A low checking frequency suits a well-diversified, long-term portfolio. But if you're actively trading, holding a single stock with high concentration risk, or approaching retirement and needing to adjust your risk weighting, the tracking frequency may need to rise accordingly. The principle is: tracking frequency should match your strategy and time horizon, not just follow habit by default.

lines: Checking your portfolio less often isn't being careless with your money - it's discipline that helps you avoid the emotional decisions that wreck a long-term strategy.
Setting a clear, scheduled check-in (say, the start of each month) instead of opening the app on a whim is a simple way to balance staying informed with keeping the calm you need.
